title: Permafrost Is Thawing From the Inside Out in Canada's North
summary: Deep in Canada's Northwest Territories, the ground is changing. Permafrost, ground that stays frozen for at least two years in a row, is thawing. In some places, it is melting from the inside out and setting off a new kind of landslide. The Mackenzie River winds through this frozen landscape. It is North America's largest northward-flowing river and drains about 20 percent of Canada's land. For thousands of years, permafrost held the region steady, but warming is crumbling that stability. In 2017 and 2018, two landslides struck the central Mackenzie Valley, moving 4.5 and 18 million cubic meters of frozen ground. The landslides carried chunks of earth that were still frozen, which had slid hundreds of meters. In 2019, geologist Joseph Young saw slopes collapsing with landslides everywhere. His team tracked ground temperatures from 2020 to 2022. They concluded that wildfires from decades earlier and rising summer temperatures had formed cracks in the ground. Water seeped in through the cracks and warmed the permafrost from below, weakening its base. The researchers named the new phenomenon permafrost detachment slides.
why_it_matters: Learning how frozen ground can melt and slide helps us understand why the places where people live and travel in the far north are changing as the Earth warms.

background_read: Permafrost is ground in cold northern places that stays frozen for years, holding the land steady like frozen glue.
In Canada's far north, the Mackenzie River winds through this frozen land, and the ground there has held firm for a very long time.
When the ground warms up, cracks can form, water can seep in, and the frozen ground can weaken and slide away.
Article_Structure: WHO: Geologist Joseph Young and his team of researchers.
WHAT: The frozen ground is melting in a new way and setting off landslides.
WHERE: In Canada's Northwest Territories, around the central Mackenzie Valley.
WHY: Wildfires from decades earlier and rising summer temperatures made cracks, and water seeping through the cracks warmed the permafrost from below.
